Summary: Resurrection hope is the Pharisaic belief, widespread by the first century, that God will raise the dead to life at the last day.
JewishBackground: The Hebrew Scriptures hint at life beyond death — Daniel's 'many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake' (Daniel 12:2) and Isaiah's 'thy dead men shall live' (Isaiah 26:19) — and by the Second Temple period the Pharisees taught resurrection openly, alongside angels and spirits, while the Sadducees denied it. Martha voices the common hope at Lazarus's tomb: 'I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day' (John 11:24). This entry covers the positive hope; the Sadducees' denial is covered in their own entry and is not repeated here.
PointsToChrist: Jesus affirms the resurrection against the Sadducees from the Torah itself — God is the God of the living — and then embodies the hope: he raises Lazarus and rises himself as 'the firstfruits of them that slept' (1 Corinthians 15:20). For the New Testament, the general resurrection Israel hoped for has begun in Christ and will be completed when all are raised.
Scripture: Daniel 12:2-3; Isaiah 26:19; Ezekiel 37:1-14; Job 19:25-27; Matthew 22:23-33; John 11:24-25; 1 Corinthians 15:20-22; Acts 23:6-8
RelatedPeople: Daniel; Isaiah; Ezekiel; Martha; Lazarus; Jesus
